pack.name: Anatomy
pack.title: The Flesh Remembers
pack.blurb: Bones, muscles, organs, nerves, hormones and the cells that build a body.

prompts.text: Name a bone in the human body.
prompts.flavor: Two hundred and six of them hold you up. The deep would like to count them.
prompts.rules: Any named bone or group of bones in the adult human body, by its everyday or anatomical name.

answers.lore: The longest and strongest bone in the body.
Named from the Greek for 'cuckoo', because it looks like a cuckoo's beak.
The smallest bone in the body, about the size of a grain of rice, deep inside the ear.
The only bone not joined to any other bone. It floats in the throat, anchoring the tongue.
A tiny bone behind the knee that has become about three times more common in humans over the last century.
Extra islands of bone in the seams of the skull. Some people have dozens.
Some people have an extra bone at the back of the skull. It was named for how often it turned up in Inca mummies.

traps.reason: Not a bone at all. It is the ulnar nerve, which is why it hurts.
Teeth are not bones, though they are harder.
Cartilage, not bone.
A bird's bone, the furcula. Humans don't have one.
A joint where three bones meet. Name one of them.
A joint. The bone you want might be the kneecap.
A joint made of eight small bones. Name one.
A joint, not a bone.
A joint, not a bone.
A joint. Say hip bone if you mean the bone.
The soft tissue inside the bones.
Connective tissue, not bone.
Nerves, not bone.
Keratin, not bone.
That's all of them at once. Name just one.
A socket built from seven bones, not a bone itself.
A soft gap between a baby's skull bones, not a bone.
Fingers and toes are built from small bones called phalanges.
A joint where finger bones meet, not a bone of its own.
The point of the elbow: part of the ulna, not a bone of its own.
The bony bump of the ankle, the end of the tibia or the fibula.
The tip of the shoulder blade, not a bone of its own.
A bump of the skull behind the ear, not a separate bone.
Part of the femur, not a separate bone.

prompts.source: Copied from the daily question "bones" on 28 November 2026.

prompts.text: Name an organ of the human body.
prompts.flavor: They work for you in the dark, unseen and unthanked. The deep knows every one of them by name.
prompts.rules: Any organ or gland of the human body, from the skin inwards, vestigial ones included, and their named parts. Tissues such as blood, and whole systems, don't count.

answers.lore: Beats about 100,000 times a day: some two and a half billion times in a long life.
About 2% of your weight, yet it burns around a fifth of your energy.
The left lung is smaller than the right, to leave room for the heart.
The only internal organ that can regrow itself. Cut down to a third of its size, it grows back.
Each one holds about a million tiny filters, and most people can live well with just one.
Its lining renews itself every few days, so that the stomach doesn't digest itself.
The body's largest organ, covering up to two square metres.
Long called useless, it may be a safe house for helpful gut bacteria.
Shaped like a butterfly, at the front of the neck.
Largest in childhood. After puberty it slowly shrinks and turns to fat.
A gland the size of a grain of rice, deep in the brain. Descartes called it the principal seat of the soul.
A temporary organ, built in pregnancy partly from the baby's tissue and partly from the mother's, then delivered after the birth.
Named from the Greek for 'snail', for its coiled shape.
All that is left of a tail. Every human embryo has a real one for a few weeks.
Folds that hold the gut in place, reclassified in 2016 as a single continuous organ.
Strictly, every bone in the body is an organ in its own right, with blood vessels and nerves of its own.
In 2018 scientists proposed that the fluid-filled spaces between tissues form one organ, perhaps the body's largest.
The pink fold in the inner corner of your eye, thought to be all that remains of a third eyelid.
Roughly one person in seven is born without this wrist muscle. Surgeons borrow its tendon for repairs elsewhere.
Tiny muscles that raise each hair into a goosebump, from ancestors who fluffed up their fur.
A small bump on the rim of some ears. Darwin took it for a trace of the pointed ears of our distant ancestors.
Clusters of insulin-making cells scattered through the pancreas, named after the student who found them in 1869.

answers.answer: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis

answers.lore: The true organ of hearing, a ribbon of hair cells coiled inside the cochlea. Alfonso Corti described it in 1851.
Snakes taste the air with theirs. In humans it is a tiny pit inside the nose, probably useless.

traps.reason: A whole system of organs. Name one of them.
A whole system of parts, not a single organ.
A tissue, and a liquid one. Not an organ.
A fluid. The glands it flows through would count.
A tissue, though it makes hormones like a gland.
A tissue, found in many organs, not one itself.
A single cell, far too small to be an organ.
Dead keratin, grown by the skin. Not an organ.
Hard keratin, grown by the skin. Not an organ.
A fluid the body makes, not an organ.
A body part, but not an organ.
A region of the body, home to many organs. Name one.
A scar, healed over in your first weeks of life. Not an organ.
The body has dozens of glands. Name one.
Trillions of microbes, sometimes called a forgotten organ. Not yours, though.
Fish have them. You, presumably, do not.
A bird's organ for storing or grinding its food. Humans make do without.
A cow's milk gland. Wrong animal.
Humans lose theirs before birth, all but a stub.
Not on humans. Not yet.
Electric eels have three. Humans have none.
A musical instrument. Wrong kind of organ.
Not an organ, whatever the poets say.
Not an organ, though it lives in one.
A region between the legs, not an organ.
Single light-sensing cells, far too small to be organs.
A sheet of tough connective tissue, not an organ.

prompts.text: Name a part of the human brain.
prompts.flavor: It weighs about three pounds and holds every thought you have ever had. Some of them were not your own.
prompts.rules: Any named part of the human brain: lobes, folds, nuclei, chambers and the membranes that wrap it. Single cells, and the nerves that leave it, don't count.

answers.lore: Latin for 'little brain'. Small as it is, it holds most of the brain's neurons.
Named after the seahorse, for its curled shape. In London cabbies it grows as they learn the city's streets.
About the size of an almond, it governs hunger, thirst, body heat and sleep.
From the Greek for 'almond', which it resembles in size and shape.
Named for its pine-cone shape. Descartes believed it was the principal seat of the soul.
A bridge of some 200 million nerve fibres joining the two halves of the brain.
Named after Paul Broca, whose patient of 1861 could say only one word: 'tan'.
Latin for 'island': a whole lobe hidden deep inside a fold of the brain.
Latin for 'black substance', for the dark pigment in its cells.
The body's master clock, perched just above where the optic nerves cross, so daylight can set it.
A ring of arteries beneath the brain, named after Thomas Willis, who described it in 1664.
The brain's vomiting centre. It sits outside the blood-brain barrier, so it can taste poisons in the blood.
Latin for 'tree of life': the white matter inside the cerebellum, which branches like a tree when cut.

answers.answer: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis

answers.lore: Francis Crick was still revising a paper about it the day he died, in 2004. He suspected it might conduct consciousness.
Latin for 'blue spot', and it really is bluish. It floods the brain with noradrenaline when alarm strikes.
Latin for 'uncertain zone'. Auguste Forel named it in 1877, saying nothing certain could be said about it.

traps.reason: The whole thing. The deep wants a piece of it.
The brain has several lobes. Name one.
The brain has hundreds of nuclei. Name one.
Joined to the brain at its base, but not part of it.
The bone around the brain, not part of it.
A single cell. The brain has some 86 billion of them.
A junction between two cells, far too small to count as a part.
Strictly an outgrowth of the brain, but it counts as a nerve, and nerves are left out.
A nerve leaving the brain, not part of it.
The fluid the brain floats in, not a part of it.
What the brain does, not a part of it.
Freud's parts of the mind, not of the brain.
Not a part of the brain, whatever Descartes thought.
A discredited 1960s theory, not a real part of the brain.
Electrical rhythms, not a part of the brain.
A computer's idea of a brain, not a part of yours.
Part of a single nerve cell, far too small to count as a part of the brain.
A chemical messenger, not a part of the brain.
A single kind of cell, far too small to count as a part.
Grown out of the brain before birth, but it belongs to the eye now.
That's the whole brain. Which part?

prompts.text: Name a muscle in the human body.
prompts.flavor: Something under the skin tightens when you read this. You did not ask it to.
prompts.rules: Any named muscle or well-known muscle group, by its anatomical or gym name.

answers.lore: The smallest skeletal muscle in the body, barely a millimetre long. It steadies the stapes, the smallest bone, to protect the inner ear from loud noise.
The tiny muscles at the root of each hair. When they tighten, the hair stands on end. It is how you get goosebumps.

traps.reason: That is connective tissue, not a muscle. It ties muscle to bone or bone to bone.
That is a region. Name a muscle found there.
Not a muscle.

prompts.flavor: Messages in the blood, sent by glands you have never seen. You obey every one.
prompts.rules: Any chemical messenger made by the human body, by its full name or its abbreviation.

answers.lore: The first hormone ever identified. In 1902 Bayliss and Starling found it in the gut, and Starling coined the very word "hormone" three years later.
Released by muscle during exercise and named in 2012 after Iris, messenger of the Greek gods. Whether it does much in humans is still argued over.

traps.reason: Made by the body, but it is not a hormone: it carries no message through the blood.
Which one? Name the hormone itself.
Not one the human body makes.

prompts.flavor: Around 100,000 kilometres of pipe, all of it inside you, none of it ever still.
prompts.rules: Any named artery or vein, or any kind of blood vessel.

answers.lore: The main feeder of the lower spinal cord, named for a Polish pathologist. Surgeons fear it: damage it during aortic surgery and the legs may be paralysed.

traps.reason: A tube or an organ, but blood does not travel through it as a vessel.
Which one? Name the vessel or the kind.

prompts.text: Name a nerve in the human body.
prompts.flavor: Every scream starts as a small electrical message. These are the wires it travels along.
prompts.rules: Any named nerve, including the twelve cranial nerves.

aliases: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

answers.answer: Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm

answers.lore: The thirteenth cranial nerve the textbooks leave out. Found in sharks in 1878 and in humans in 1913, it sits ahead of the first, so it is numbered zero.
A twig of the vagus that reaches the ear canal. It is why cleaning your ear can make you cough. Aldermen were said to tickle it to revive their appetite at feasts.

traps.reason: Which one? Name the nerve itself.
Not a nerve.

prompts.text: Name a part of the eye or the ear.
prompts.flavor: You are reading this with one of them. Something may be listening with the other.
prompts.rules: Any named structure of the human eye or ear, inside or out.

answers.lore: A layer of the cornea just 15 thousandths of a millimetre thick, announced in 2013 by Harminder Dua. Anatomy was still finding new parts of you.

traps.reason: Close by, but not part of either one.
That is the whole thing. Name a part of it.

prompts.text: Name a type of cell found in the human body.
prompts.flavor: Thirty-seven trillion of them agreed to be you. Not one of them was asked.
prompts.rules: Any named kind of human cell, by its everyday or scientific name.

answers.lore: Taken without consent from Henrietta Lacks in 1951, these cancer cells never stopped dividing. They helped test the polio vaccine and still fill labs worldwide.

traps.reason: That is a part of a cell, or the word itself. Name a kind of cell.
Found in or on you, perhaps, but it is not a human cell.

prompts.text: Name a medical specialty or kind of specialist doctor.
prompts.flavor: For every part of you there is someone who studied nothing else. Some of them enjoyed it.
prompts.rules: Any recognised branch of medicine or surgery, as the field or as the doctor who practises it.

answers.lore: The medicine of the bends, rapture of the deep and oxygen under pressure. Doctors who sink for a living: the abyss approves.

traps.reason: A health profession in its own right, but not a medical specialty a doctor trains in.
Which kind? Name the specialty.
Different patients, different degree.
